title: Ramesh Chauhan's Year of Tasting Sessions for Thums Up
dek: When Coca-Cola left India in 1977, Ramesh Chauhan of Parle spent more than a year getting the taste of a new cola right, then sold it to Coca-Cola in 1993.

story.event: Developing an Indian cola after Coca-Cola's 1977 exit, using a trained staff tasting panel
story.summary: After Coca-Cola left India in 1977 rather than dilute its stake under the Foreign Exchange Regulation Act, Ramesh Chauhan of the family firm Parle, whose earlier Gluco Cola had been forced off the market by a Coca-Cola trademark suit, developed Thums Up over more than a year, training his own staff to describe flavours. The cola came to dominate India's soft-drink market; in 1993 Chauhan sold it and four other brands to Coca-Cola.
paragraphs: In 1977 India's new Janata government, with George Fernandes as industry minister, enforced a rule that foreign companies cut their stakes in their Indian operations to 40 per cent. More than 35 companies left rather than comply. Among them was Coca-Cola, by far the country's best-selling soft drink. Rivals rushed in: Crown Cola, King Cola, Double Seven, Campa Cola.

At Parle in Bombay, Ramesh Chauhan had reason to be wary of colas. He had joined the family firm in 1962 with an engineering degree from MIT. Parle's first soft drink, Gluco Cola, launched in 1949, had been taken to court by Coca-Cola over the word cola; renamed Parle Cola, he later said, "the product was dead." Parle had since built Gold Spot, an orange drink, and Limca, a lemon soda. Now Chauhan set out to make a cola of his own.

It took him more than a year, and the hardest part was taste. "Tasting sessions would always throw up conflicting and confusing replies," he told Outlook Business in 2013. So he picked people from Parle's own staff and trained them to put flavours into words: "We didn't want just 'achcha hai'." Samples were served cool rather than cold so that each flavour stood out, and drew on cinnamon, cardamom, nutmeg, vanilla and citrus oils; the tasters' feedback let him cut the formula to fewer ingredients. The result was fizzier than Coca-Cola and not too sweet. An advertising agency proposed the name, which, marketing lore has it, Chauhan doubted people would read as encouragement.

Parle spent heavily on launch advertising, and Chauhan said the business "really took off" after Coca-Cola's exit. Within 15 years, industry people told Outlook, the cola held 60 per cent of India's soft-drink market. Then Pepsi arrived in 1990 and Coca-Cola's return looked certain. Worried that his franchised bottlers would defect, Chauhan sold Thums Up, Limca, Gold Spot, Maaza and Citra to Coca-Cola in 1993, and wept at the signing in Atlanta. He later said Coca-Cola tried to kill the cola, a charge the company has denied; in 2021 its sales passed $1 billion.

quote.text: To son and wife, to brother and friend, give not power over thee while thou livest; and give not thy goods to another, lest thou repent and make supplication for them again.
quote.work: Ecclesiasticus (The Wisdom of Ben Sira) and the Wisdom of Solomon
quote.source_title: The Wisdom of the Apocrypha, Project Gutenberg eBook #77250
quote.connection: Ben Sira tells a householder not to hand over his goods while he lives, lest he come back pleading for them. Chauhan had sound reasons to sell, and Thums Up outlived the neglect he later described; yet he wept at the signing. Whether keeping it would have been wiser stays open.

reflection: Most feedback arrives as achcha hai: it's fine, it's good, carry on. It is kind, and it tells you almost nothing. Chauhan's answer was not to look for better tasters but to train the ones he had, giving them words for what their tongues already noticed.

You can do something similar with the people around you. A colleague who calls a report fine may well have felt the paragraph that dragged, and simply lacks the habit of saying so. A narrower question often brings out the answer that was there all along.
invitation: Choose one piece of work that someone recently called fine. Ask them a single narrow question about it, such as which part they would cut first, and write down exactly what they say.

cross_checks.claim: Coca-Cola left India in 1977 under pressure from the Janata government and industry minister George Fernandes.
Parle's earlier Gluco Cola was challenged by Coca-Cola over the word cola and failed as Parle Cola.
Chauhan created Thums Up to fill the gap left by Coca-Cola's 1977 exit, and Parle's business took off afterwards.
Chauhan sold Thums Up and other Parle brands to Coca-Cola in 1993.

research_notes: Timing: Business Today (2022) and most accounts date Thums Up's launch to 1977, while Outlook Business says the cola took Chauhan more than a year to develop; the two are hard to reconcile if work began only after Coca-Cola's exit, so the story says it took more than a year without giving a launch month, and approx_date stays 1977. The tasting-panel account rests on Chauhan's recollection to Outlook Business (2013) and is attributed. The name's origin with an ad agency and Chauhan's doubts are 'marketing folklore' in Outlook's own words, so the story marks it as lore. Launch advertising: Outlook cites ad-industry veterans' estimate of at least Rs 20 lakh; the story says only that Parle spent heavily (Chauhan told Business Standard in 1997 that Parle had the highest ad spend of Indian companies). Market share: the 60% figure is 'industry people' quoted by Outlook and is attributed as such. Sale: Outlook lists five brands (Thums Up, Gold Spot, Limca, Maaza, Citra); Business Today (2022) lists four and says the acquisition completed by 1995; the story follows Outlook's five and the 1993 date. No price is given because neither loadable source states one (a widely repeated $60 million figure was not confirmed). Coca-Cola's neglect of Thums Up is Chauhan's claim; Outlook notes Coca-Cola has consistently denied it. Exit reason: Outlook gives the FERA 40% rule; some accounts add a demand to disclose the formula, which no loadable source here confirms, so the story leaves it out. A 2013 Pioneer profile (now offline) credited Chauhan with his brother Prakash Chauhan and Parle executive Bhanu Vakil; the loadable sources credit Ramesh Chauhan alone, so the founder field names him. Arc: Parle already made soft drinks, so the episode is its move back into cola after the 1950s failure. Ben Sira's advice concerns a householder keeping control of his property while he lives (chapter 33, verses 19-20 in the usual numbering); it is applied here by analogy to the 1993 sale.
